docs.title: rocm-bake
docs.text:
Reproducible builds of PyTorch, Triton, AITER, CuPy, NIXL, vLLM and LMCache against ROCm, on a three-node BuildKit fleet, with every artifact published to a local OCI registry.

The build is one docker buildx bake file and one Makefile. Everything else in the repository exists to make that build fast, repeatable, and measurable.

docs.title: What it builds
docs.text:
PyTorch compiled from source against ROCm, with Triton, AITER, CuPy, NIXL, vLLM and LMCache on top, for gfx950 (default), gfx1201 and gfx1250.

Every pinned version is on the bake variables page, generated from rocm-bake.hcl — the single source for every value a build reads. make list-vars prints what is actually in effect, and make version-check compares it against the latest upstream releases and against the wheels published in the registry.

docs.title: Conventions in this documentation
docs.text:
Commands are run from the repository root on snoc-strix unless stated otherwise. make help lists every target; targets marked * build and push to the registry, which needs the ci login.

The repository is at sbates130272/rocm-bake and is MIT licensed.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: From nothing to a published PyTorch image. On a fleet that is already set up, skip to step 5.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• All nodes on the same Tailscale network.
  • snoc-strix: a gfx1151 GPU, Docker 27+. Runs the Zot registry, the shared compiler cache, and the GPU tests.
  • snoc-thinkstation, snoc-gaming: Docker 27+, reachable as ssh <host> from Strix. Both are gfx1201 (RDNA4): they cross-compile for gfx950 fine but cannot run the test stage.
  • 200 GB+ of disk per node for the BuildKit cache.
docker --version
docker buildx version

The tailnet must bypass the corporate proxy

HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY are set in this environment but no_proxy is not, so every proxy-aware tool — curl, Python's urllib, and the Go binaries including docker — tries to reach snoc-* through ZScaler and fails. The Makefile exports a NO_PROXY_LIST for its own targets, but anything you run by hand needs the same in your shell profile:

export no_proxy=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1,.ts.net,.local,10.0.0.0/8,100.64.0.0/10
export NO_PROXY="$no_proxy"

docs.title: Step 1 — Clone
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:sbates130272/rocm-bake.git
cd rocm-bake

docs.title: Step 2 — Check Zot
docs.text:
Zot is the local OCI registry. It holds the published images, the BuildKit layer cache as OCI artifacts, and a pull-through mirror of Docker Hub, GHCR and Quay. It already runs on Strix as a bare-metal systemd service (zot.service, configured in /etc/zot/config.json), deployed and owned outside this repository.

Do not start a second one

Other services on the fleet pull through the same registry. Nothing in this repository starts, stops or configures Zot — the zot-* targets only inspect it.

make zot-check      # is it active and answering?
make zot-catalog    # what does it hold?

Anonymous read is open, so every pull, pull-through and cache read works unauthenticated. Only pushing needs the ci account from /etc/zot/htpasswd.

Store that credential with pass, which is GPG-encrypted at rest and works over SSH. The secretservice helper does not: it fails with Cannot create an item in a locked collection whenever the gnome-keyring login collection has not been unlocked by a graphical session.

sudo apt-get install -y pass golang-docker-credential-helpers
pass init <your-gpg-key-id>        # gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long
# set "credsStore": "pass" in ~/.docker/config.json
docker login snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080 -u ci
docker-credential-pass list        # verify it landed

One login on Strix covers the whole fleet: buildx sends registry auth from your local Docker config to the builder as a session attachment, so builds pushing from think or gaming use it too.

Zot also needs a raised HTTP read timeout, or pushing the ROCm base fails — its largest layer is 8.67 GB and cannot cross a 1 Gb/s link inside Zot's 60-second default. In /etc/zot/config.json:

"http": {
  "readTimeout": "30m",
  "writeTimeout": "30m"
}

then sudo systemctl restart zot. See Troubleshooting for what the failure looks like if you skip this.

The registry serves plain HTTP over the tailnet, so the Docker daemon needs it in /etc/docker/daemon.json (already set on Strix):

{
  "insecure-registries": ["snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080"],
  "registry-mirrors": ["http://snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080"]
}

docs.title: Step 3 — Create the builders
docs.text:
make builder-snoc-strix     # local, gfx1151, hosts Zot + sccache
make builder-snoc-think     # snoc-thinkstation, over SSH
make builder-snoc-gaming    # snoc-gaming, over SSH
make builder-status         # what exists now

The remote nodes join over SSH to their Docker daemons: buildx creates and owns a buildkit container on each, so neither needs buildkitd, TLS certificates, or the buildx plugin installed.

Every builder is created with .builders/buildkitd-strix.toml and --driver-opt network=host. Both are load-bearing:

  • the config carries plain HTTP to Zot, the pull-through mirrors, and a [dns] block, because BuildKit writes its own /etc/resolv.conf for the build sandbox and defaults it to 8.8.8.8 — without the block a RUN step cannot resolve any tailnet name;
  • network=host gives the builder container the host's resolver, MagicDNS included. Docker strips loopback nameservers when it writes a bridged container's resolv.conf.

Both are fixed at create time

An existing builder does not pick up edits to the toml. After changing it: docker buildx rm snoc-strix && make builder-snoc-strix.

docs.title: Step 4 — Deploy the shared compiler cache
docs.text:
Every build container runs its own sccache server, and all of them share one object store: nginx with the WebDAV modules, serving a plain directory tree on Strix at :8081. An object compiled on any node is a hit on the others.

sudo ./.builders/deploy-webdav.sh
make cache-check                 # can every node reach it?
make cache-summary               # endpoint, size, disk, deltas, hit rates

Why a durable store, and why WebDAV

The store has to survive a reboot. An in-RAM store loses the whole fleet's compiler cache on a power cycle, and an overflow tier does not help — it is not durable storage and is never read back at startup. A plain directory tree survives, can be backed up with rsync, and is bounded only by the filesystem.

WebDAV rather than S3/MinIO because dl.min.io is blocked by the corporate proxy and MinIO is not packaged, whereas nginx-extras is a normal apt install and sccache speaks WebDAV natively.

There is nothing to install on the other nodes. .builders/deploy-sccache.sh installs a node-level sccache daemon on port 4226; builds do not use it, and it is only for compiling on a host directly.

docs.title: Step 5 — Build
docs.text:
make build-pytorch                    # one target on $(BUILDER)
make build-all                        # every target, one builder
make push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool       # scheduled across all three nodes

BUILDER=snoc-pool is a sentinel, not a buildx builder: it routes the request through the balancer, which runs one bake per target on a chosen node and hands results between them through Zot.

Each make build-* runs through telemetry/build.sh, which records duration, layer-cache hit ratio and sccache counters, then exits with the build's own status. TELEMETRY=0 make build-pytorch skips it.

The build refuses to start when the compiler-cache store is unreachable, rather than silently spending an hour recompiling everything:

docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl --set '*.args.REQUIRE_SCCACHE=0' pytorch

docs.title: Watch it
docs.text:
From a second terminal:

make watch                              # every builder, with a live tail
make watch WATCH_BUILDERS=snoc-think WATCH_LINES=40

Or one thing at a time:

make build-status     # records on $(BUILDER): running, completed, errored
make build-logs       # step output; BUILD=<id> for a specific record
make build-inspect    # duration, steps, cached steps, VCS revision
make builder-logs     # buildkitd's own log: registry, DNS, cache failures
make build-stop       # cancel builds started from this repo

build-logs is what the build's steps printed. builder-logs is the daemon underneath, and that is where a registry fault, a DNS fault or a cache fault shows up — often while the build itself merely looks slow.

docs.title: Step 6 — Verify
docs.text:
make gpu-test GPU_HOST=snoc-thinkstation PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH=gfx1201

gpu-test runs the published image on a machine with a real GPU and checks per-dtype numerics. It exists because a BuildKit RUN step has no /dev/kfd, so nothing inside the build graph can prove the image works — and an incorrect HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION once shipped undetected in every image.

By hand:

docker run --rm -it --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri \
  snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950

import torch
print(torch.__version__)           # 2.15.0+rocm10.1
print(torch.cuda.is_available())   # True
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

docs.title: Step 7 — Measure it
docs.text:
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=cold BUILDER=snoc-think
make bench-report

See Performance for what the four scenarios mean and how to read the numbers.

docs.title: Node roles
docs.text:
snoc-strix is the default BUILDER and hosts both shared services. Its GPU is gfx1151; no node in the fleet has a gfx950 card, which is the default build target, so make test — the in-graph test stage — only proves anything when PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH matches the hardware it runs on. make gpu-test can drive any host with a GPU and /dev/kfd, which on this fleet means matching the arch to the host.

snoc-think and snoc-gaming are build capacity. They are joined to buildx over SSH to their Docker daemons, so buildx creates and owns a buildkit container on each: neither needs buildkitd, TLS certificates, or the buildx plugin installed. Both are gfx1201 (RDNA4). They cross-compile for gfx950 without difficulty — compiling for an architecture does not require having one — but cannot run the test stage.

snoc-pool is not a node. It is a sentinel: BUILDER=snoc-pool routes the request through .builders/balance.sh instead of to a buildx builder. A buildx multi-node builder does exist and can be created with make builder-snoc-pool, but nothing is built against it now, which is why make watch skips it — its build records never update. See the balancer.

docs.title: Why a tailnet
docs.text:
The three machines are not on one LAN, and the corporate proxy must never see tailnet traffic. Two consequences run through everything else:

  • no_proxy has to include .ts.net or every proxy-aware tool fails against snoc-*. The Makefile exports it; interactive shells need it in a profile.
  • Name resolution inside a build container is not the node's. BuildKit writes its own resolv.conf for the build sandbox and defaults it to a public resolver, so .builders/buildkitd-strix.toml carries a [dns] block listing MagicDNS first and two public resolvers after it. The public entries are load-bearing, not belt-and-braces: this tailnet has no global nameservers, so MagicDNS SERVFAILs on anything outside it and apt, pip and the PyTorch clone would all fail.

Even that was not enough for the compiler cache. Under load a tailnet lookup falls through to a public resolver, which answers NXDOMAIN, after which the search domain is appended and the query becomes snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net.fold-leaffish.ts.net. That cost 79 of 361 compiles in one Triton build — objects compiled and then thrown away. So the Makefile resolves the store's hostname to an address once, on the host, and the build containers address it by IP. The name stays the configuration surface; only containers see an address.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text: Piece What it is Owned here? rocm-bake.hcl The build graph: 13 targets, 3 groups, 45 variables Yes Makefile A wrapper that reads every default out of rocm-bake.hcl Yes docker/Dockerfile.* Nine Dockerfiles; the build context is always the repo root Yes telemetry/build.sh Wraps a bake, emits Prometheus metrics, exits with bake's status Yes .builders/* Node setup, the balancer, the benchmark harness, registry readers Yes Zot OCI registry: images, layer cache, pull-through mirror No — zot.service nginx WebDAV sccache object store Deployed by .builders/deploy-webdav.sh node_exporter Scrapes the telemetry textfile on :9100 No

docs.title: Single source of truth
docs.text:
rocm-bake.hcl owns every value a build reads. The Makefile does not keep a copy of any of them: it parses the variable blocks at make parse time and reads the defaults out. This matters because the two used to disagree silently — a make target and a bare docker buildx bake would have built different images from the same tree, and nothing would have said so.

.builders/check-defaults.py enforces it in CI. It fails the build if a bake default is re-declared in the Makefile, if the Makefile reads a variable rocm-bake.hcl does not define, if $(call bake,…) names a target that does not exist, or if WHEEL_REPOS drifts from the wheels group.

The same pattern applies to the serving stack: serving/docker-compose.yml owns the runtime defaults, and the Makefile reads ${NAME:-default} out of it.

docs.title: Build graph
docs.text:
rocm-bake.hcl declares thirteen targets. Bake derives the build DAG from the contexts each one names, and orders the graph itself — which is why asking for vllm alone also builds pytorch-base, triton-wheel, pytorch, aiter-wheel, nixl-wheel, cupy-wheel and lmcache-wheel, in dependency order.

flowchart TD
    base["pytorch-base<br/><i>rocm/dev-ubuntu-26.04:10.1.0-full</i>"]
    triton["triton-wheel<br/><i>noarch</i>"]
    cupy["cupy-wheel"]
    pt["pytorch"]
    ptw["pytorch-wheel"]
    run["pytorch-run"]
    test["pytorch-test"]
    aiter["aiter-wheel"]
    nixl["nixl-wheel<br/><i>+ UCX from source</i>"]
    lmc["lmcache"]
    lmcw["lmcache-wheel"]
    vllm["vllm"]
    vllmw["vllm-wheel"]

    base --> triton
    base --> cupy
    base --> pt
    triton --> pt
    pt --> ptw
    pt --> run
    pt --> test
    pt --> aiter
    triton --> aiter
    pt --> nixl
    pt --> lmc
    triton --> lmc
    nixl --> lmc
    cupy --> lmc
    lmc --> lmcw
    pt --> vllm
    triton --> vllm
    aiter --> vllm
    nixl --> vllm
    lmcw --> vllm
    vllm --> vllmw

Four edges are worth explaining because they are not obvious from the names.

triton-wheel builds from the base, not from pytorch. Triton needs cmake<4 while PyTorch pulls cmake 4.x, so they cannot share an environment. That also means Triton can build in parallel with PyTorch on another node. It is the only target with no architecture in its tag: Triton is a compiler and publishes one noarch wheel.

cupy-wheel hangs off the base too, because CuPy has no torch dependency. It is not optional. LMCache's multi-process server imports cupy at module scope to build a cupy.cuda.ExternalStream, and no published wheel fits this stack — PyPI's cupy-rocm-7-0 targets a different ROCm major, and plain cupy ships only an sdist. Without it the server dies on the first request and vLLM waits five minutes before reporting a generic engine failure.

vllm consumes lmcache-wheel. vLLM ships the LMCache MP connector but imports lmcache.utils from it, so the wheel has to exist first. On the scheduled path it has to be published first, not merely building somewhere else.

lmcache takes no AITER context. Its extension is cache movement, not GEMMs, and it has no AITER code path.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Group Members default pytorch-base, pytorch, pytorch-wheel, triton-wheel, aiter-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel wheels pytorch-wheel, triton-wheel, aiter-wheel, nixl-wheel, cupy-wheel, vllm-wheel, lmcache-wheel serving cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel

There is no all group. Two targets are deliberately outside default:

  • pytorch-test cannot run inside the build graph at all. Its stage exits 1 when torch.cuda.is_available() is false, and a BuildKit RUN step has no /dev/kfd. It is a verification step for a finished image on a real GPU (make test on a GPU node), and including it in default made build-all and push-all fail at the last target every time.
  • pytorch-run is excluded because no node currently has a usable GPU to exercise the runtime image on, and building it every run costs time and a registry push for an artifact nobody can test. make push-runtime still builds it, and it belongs back in default once a GPU node is available.

docs.title: How inputs are wired
docs.text:
Targets take their inputs from sibling targets through target: named contexts. That is bake's dependency mechanism and the only one it has.

contexts = USE_PUB ? {} : {
  triton-wheels = "target:triton-wheel"
  base-img      = "target:pytorch-base"
}
args = {
  TRITON_WHEEL_IMAGE = USE_PUB ? PUB_TRITON : "triton-wheels"
  BASE_IMAGE         = USE_PUB ? PUB_BASE   : "base-img"
}

A target with no context on its inputs is, as far as bake is concerned, independent — and may run concurrently with the thing it needs.

docs.title: PUBLISHED_INPUTS
docs.text:
Set PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1 and every one of those contexts collapses to a registry reference instead. The PUB_* locals in rocm-bake.hcl hold those references, and they must track the tags of the target they mirror — a change to one is a change to the other.

This is what makes cross-node scheduling possible. A target: context only works within one bake invocation, so one-bake-per-node would rebuild the whole chain on every node rather than pulling what the previous stage just pushed.

pytorch-run is the exception: its context has to resolve in both modes, so it uses a docker-image:// reference.

Note

PUBLISHED_INPUTS is read by bake from the environment, so it needs PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1 make …, not make … PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1. The same is true of SCCACHE_LOG, RUN_ID, CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX and the SDE_* overrides.

docs.title: The balancer
docs.text:
buildx's multi-node builder does not balance. Node selection is driven by platform matching, and when every node advertises linux/amd64 the choice among them ignores capacity: all five targets once landed on snoc-gaming (16 cores, 15 GB) while snoc-think (32 cores, 122 GB) sat idle. There is no hook to change that, so the scheduling happens in .builders/balance.sh instead — one bake invocation per target, each pinned to a builder it picks.

make push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool       # the usual way to build everything
make push-wheels BUILDER=snoc-pool    # just the wheel artifacts
.builders/balance.sh --dry-run        # what it would schedule, and where
.builders/balance.sh --best           # the strongest node right now

Nodes are scored by free GB of RAM plus idle cores, weighted equally on purpose: a cold PyTorch build runs one cc1plus per core and each takes 1–2 GB, so RAM is what actually bounds a big node. Nodes below MIN_MEM_GB (default 8) are skipped.

Work is scheduled from the dependency graph, not from a list kept beside it. .builders/depgraph.py asks bake for each target's contexts — the same target: edges that define the build DAG — and balance.sh starts a target once every dependency inside the run has finished and been pushed.

.builders/depgraph.py --deps pytorch vllm-wheel
# pytorch pytorch-base triton-wheel
# vllm-wheel aiter-wheel lmcache-wheel nixl-wheel pytorch triton-wheel

What to build is a set, and ordering takes care of itself:

TARGETS="pytorch-wheel triton-wheel" .builders/balance.sh

It defaults to bake's default group. make push-wheels uses the wheels group plus pytorch and pytorch-base, because every wheel builds FROM one or both of those and neither is a wheel.

This replaced a hand-written STAGE_1..STAGE_5. That list was a second copy of what rocm-bake.hcl already stated, and the two could drift without anything saying so: a gfx1250 run scheduled vllm-wheel when no gfx1250 pytorch image existed anywhere, and it died resolving that base image at step 1 of 7, 0 s in, taking the rest of its node's queue with it.

Three orderings the old stages asserted by hand are now edges in rocm-bake.hcl, enforced by construction:

  • triton-wheel before pytorch — the pytorch image installs that wheel
  • lmcache-wheel before vllm-wheel — vLLM takes a lmcache-wheel context, and results cross nodes through Zot, so it must be published first
  • pytorch-base before everything

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
Before any build starts, every image the run resolves from the registry — minus the ones it publishes itself — is checked against Zot. A missing input is named up front, with the make target that creates it, instead of surfacing as a target dying at step 1 after the scheduler has already committed work to a node.

depgraph: these images are needed but not published, and nothing in
this run builds them:
  …/rocm-pytorch/pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx1250
      needed by: aiter-wheel, lmcache-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm-wheel
   build it with: make push-pytorch

Only a 404 counts as absent. The corporate proxy answers 403 for the tailnet unless no_proxy covers it, and blocking a build on that would be wrong.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text:
Among the targets eligible at any moment, the longest goes to the node that would finish it soonest, and each node runs one build at a time — several concurrent builds on one box each derive MAX_JOBS from MemAvailable as though they were alone, and oversubscribe it.

The packing cost model is .builders/target-costs, and it ranks by which node would finish a target soonest rather than which is least loaded, because this fleet's upload speeds span a factor of 25.

--queue is still accepted and ignored. It named the mode that dropped stage barriers entirely, which was safe only while nothing in a run depended on anything else in it; dependency ordering supersedes it, and callers still passing it get the better behaviour rather than an unknown-argument error mid-build.

docs.title: Why build-all refuses the pool
docs.text:
make build-all BUILDER=snoc-pool exits with an error rather than scheduling. Scheduling makes every target its own bake invocation, so they cannot hand results to each other through target: contexts — stage 2 would build against whatever happens to be in the registry rather than what stage 1 just produced, silently. On a single builder the contexts resolve in-process and it is fine.

make push-all  BUILDER=snoc-pool    # scheduled, publishes
make build-all BUILDER=snoc-think   # single builder, no push

docs.title: MAX_JOBS
docs.text:
Left empty, each build derives its own job count from the node it lands on, sized by MemAvailable rather than by core count, with a per-job memory budget of 2 GB. Set MAX_JOBS to pin one.

The derivation is sampled when the compile step starts, by which point the build's own earlier steps have taken memory of their own. A cold PyTorch that settled at 21 GB available still derived 5 jobs, where the same node gives a hot run 10 — because a hot run's early steps are all cache hits. The derivation therefore tracks how much work precedes the compile, which differs by scenario. That is why the benchmark harness keys its results by job count and can pin it.

docs.title: Telling builds apart
docs.text:
Every target stamps rocm-pytorch-build/<target>/<arch>/<RUN_ID> into its BuildKit history record. RUN_ID defaults to dev.

The prefix is this repository's name rather than something shorter because a sibling project builds on the same nodes, uses the same convention, and produces images with the same names — pytorch, triton, aiter. A shared prefix made its builds indistinguishable from these in make watch.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Four caches sit between a make build-pytorch and a from-scratch compile. They are independent: a Dockerfile edit can drop layer reuse to 5% while sccache still serves every compile, and a changed compiler flag can do the opposite.

flowchart LR
    build["a build step"]
    local["<b>1. BuildKit content store</b><br/>per node, local disk<br/>gckeepstorage 100GB"]
    layer["<b>2. Layer cache</b><br/>OCI artifacts in Zot<br/>two-tier: rolling + -ref"]
    sccache["<b>3. sccache</b><br/>nginx WebDAV on Strix :8081<br/>object files, fleet-wide"]
    pull["<b>4. Pull-through</b><br/>Zot mirrors Docker Hub,<br/>GHCR and Quay"]

    build --> local --> layer
    build --> sccache
    build --> pull

Each one is removed by a different lever, which is exactly what the benchmark scenarios are built on.

docs.title: 1. The node's content store
docs.text: BuildKit keeps every blob it has pulled or produced on the node's own disk, bounded by gckeepstorage = "100GB" in .builders/buildkitd-strix.toml. Nothing in this repository manages it; docker buildx prune is the only lever, and it is shared with any other project building on that node.

docs.title: 2. The layer cache, in Zot
docs.text:
Each target exports its layers as OCI artifacts to a *-cache repository in Zot, so a layer built on one node is reusable from any of them.

Target Cache repository pytorch-base base-cache pytorch, pytorch-wheel pytorch-cache triton-wheel triton-wheel-cache aiter-wheel aiter-wheel-cache pytorch-run runtime-cache cupy-wheel cupy-wheel-cache nixl-wheel nixl-wheel-cache vllm, vllm-wheel vllm-cache lmcache, lmcache-wheel lmcache-cache

docs.title: Two tiers
docs.text:
Reads always consult two refs: the rolling tag, and a frozen -ref baseline. Writes go to the rolling tag unless CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX=-ref, which is how the baseline is deliberately refreshed.

# Refresh the known-good baseline from a build you trust
CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX=-ref make push-pytorch

Without the second tier, one bad build overwrites the only cache everyone reads.

docs.title: Scoped by architecture
docs.text:
Image tags have carried the architecture since ARCH_TAG landed, but the cache refs did not: every arch-sensitive target wrote <repo>-cache:latest. A gfx1201 build overwrote the gfx950 cache with layers gfx950 can never hit, and the next gfx950 build rebuilt cold and did the same back — so alternating architectures cost two cold builds, every time. CACHE_ARCH scopes those refs now, and arches-* is safe to repeat.

pytorch-base and triton-wheel stay on the shared, unscoped ref deliberately. Neither takes PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH, Triton is a compiler that publishes one noarch wheel, and both are built once for the whole fleet.

Arch-sensitive targets currently read a third ref as well: the old unscoped latest, kept transitionally so the pre-CACHE_ARCH cache is not wasted. It is marked for deletion once each architecture in ARCHES has been built at least once.

Cache exports fail silently

Every cache-to carries ignore-error=true. A registry that is down, full, or refusing the push does not fail the build — it just means the next build has nothing to read. make builder-logs is where that shows up; the build itself only looks slow next time.

Inspect reuse with:

make layer-summary    # per image, most recent build, with the node it ran on
make build-inspect    # one build: duration, steps, cached steps

docs.title: 3. The compiler cache
docs.text:
Every build container runs its own sccache server, and all of them share one object store: nginx with the WebDAV modules serving a plain directory tree at /var/cache/sccache-webdav on Strix, port 8081. An object compiled on any node is a hit on the others.

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT     http://<resolved-ip>:8081
SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX   rocm-pytorch
SCCACHE_SERVER_UDS          /tmp/sccache.sock
CMAKE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER   sccache
CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER sccache
CMAKE_HIP_COMPILER_LAUNCHER sccache
HIP_CLANG_LAUNCHER          /usr/local/bin/sccache

sccache intercepts compiler invocations, caches object files by a hash of source plus flags, and returns the cached object when both match.

Three constraints make this work, and each one fails quietly if broken.

A shared server is impossible. sccache's client sends a path, and the server reads and hashes the file itself. A server on the host cannot see a build container's sources — every compile dies with No such file or directory. Only the storage layer can be shared.

The server is addressed over a unix socket, not a TCP port. The builders run with network=host, so a fixed SCCACHE_SERVER_PORT would be shared fleet-wide: a Triton build's client once connected to a concurrent PyTorch build's sccache server, which then could not see the files it was asked to hash. SCCACHE_SERVER_UDS=/tmp/sccache.sock removes the possibility. There is deliberately no SCCACHE_SERVER_PORT variable in rocm-bake.hcl.

The store is addressed by IP, not by name. See the tailnet DNS problem. The Makefile resolves SCCACHE_WEBDAV_HOST once on the host and exports the resolved form as SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT. A consequence worth knowing: setting SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT yourself only takes effect for a bare bake, because the Makefile exports its own value unconditionally.

docs.title: Refusing to build uncached
docs.text:
docker/Dockerfile.pytorch probes the store at image build time and refuses to start a compile when it is unreachable, rather than spending an hour rebuilding everything from scratch:

docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl --set '*.args.REQUIRE_SCCACHE=0' pytorch

The build prints sccache --show-stats as its last action, which is where the telemetry wrapper reads the counters from. They cannot be queried afterwards: the sccache server lives and dies with the build container.

docs.title: Inspecting the store
docs.text:
make cache-summary    # endpoint, size, disk, deltas, hit rates
make cache-check      # can every build node reach it?
make cache-logs       # the WebDAV access log

cache-summary prints a delta and a rate as well as the totals, because totals alone say nothing about the build in front of you — objects arriving is the number that moves while a build runs, and "+412 objects" means something very different over eight seconds than over an hour.

The hit rate does not come from the store. WebDAV has no stats verb, so the store can report its size and object count and nothing else; sccache prints --show-stats at the end of each build step, telemetry/build.sh parses that into rocm_build_sccache_hit_ratio, and cache-summary reads it back per target from the textfile collector.

docs.title: Isolating a run
docs.text: SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX is a directory in the store, so a benchmark or an experiment can run against an isolated namespace and delete it afterwards without touching the fleet's objects. The benchmark harness does exactly this for its frozen and cold runs.

docs.title: 4. Pull-through
docs.text: .builders/buildkitd-strix.toml points docker.io, ghcr.io and quay.io at Zot, which syncs them on demand. The ROCm base image is 8.67 GB in a single layer, so this is the difference between a build that starts in seconds and one that starts after a WAN transfer — which is precisely what the frozen scenario measures.

docs.title: What each one is worth
docs.text: That question has a measured answer rather than an estimated one. See Performance.

docs.title: Multiple GFX targets
docs.text:
Two different things, easy to confuse:

What it produces PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH='gfx950;gfx1201' One fat build, both code objects in one binary, one set of tags ARCHES='gfx950 gfx1201' Two builds, two separately-tagged sets of artifacts

PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH picks the architecture for one build and defaults to the single value gfx950. ARCHES is the list the arches-* wrappers fan out over, and defaults to gfx950 gfx1201 gfx1250.

make arches-push-all                      # every target, every arch
make arches-push-wheels                   # just the wheel artifacts
make arches-build-pytorch ARCHES=gfx1201  # narrow it while iterating
make arches-list                          # what ARCHES resolves to

arches-% is a pattern rule: it accepts any target name, not only the examples above. Each architecture is a full pass over every target, so treat the list as a multiplier on build time. The passes run sequentially — they contend for the same three builders and the same compiler cache, so running them concurrently only makes both slower.

docs.title: gfx1250 is in the list without being in the fleet
docs.text:
The builders cross-compile — no node has a gfx950 card, yet the fleet builds gfx950 every day — so having no such card only means make test and make gpu-test cannot cover it. The ROCm 10.1 toolchain in the base image compiles it:

clang -x hip --offload-arch=gfx1250 -nogpulib -c   # exits 0

docs.title: gfx1250 is not RDNA, despite the number
docs.text:
This is the one place the architecture naming actively misleads, and the build branches on it.

AITER's kernel prebuild is CDNA-only in practice, so PREBUILD_LEVEL is chosen from the architecture rather than fixed. On gfx1201 every one of the 13 844 kernels compiled and the build then failed in the JIT module phase: 6 of 68 modules carry CDNA-only code — MFMA templates, GFX9 DPP broadcasts ("broadcasts are not supported on GFX10+"), CDNA inline asm, gfx950/ header trees — and setup.py treats a failed module as fatal. bdist_wheel exited 1 after 51 minutes and produced no wheel. Reproduced twice. Upstream documents it: AITER lists gfx1201 as Experimental, with most CK and ASM kernels CDNA-only.

So RDNA gets level 0. Those six modules cannot run there whatever we do, every other module stays reachable because AITER JIT-compiles on first use, and the prebuild is a startup-latency optimisation rather than a capability. A wheel that exists beats a faster first inference that never happens.

The detection has to special-case gfx125x:

ARCH_RDNA_TEST = replace(PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH, "gfx125", "")
IS_RDNA = (
  ARCH_RDNA_TEST != replace(ARCH_RDNA_TEST, "gfx11", "") ||
  ARCH_RDNA_TEST != replace(ARCH_RDNA_TEST, "gfx12", "")
)
PREBUILD_LEVEL = PREBUILD_KERNELS != "" ? PREBUILD_KERNELS : (IS_RDNA ? "0" : "2")

gfx1250 and gfx1251 are gfx12-numbered but are MI450-class datacenter parts, not RDNA: upstream LLVM gates amdgpu-sched-strategy=coexec on gfx1250 and gfx950 together, and gives gfx1250 tensor instructions no RDNA part has. Left to the bare gfx12 test they would read as RDNA and silently drop the kernel prebuild to level 0 — turning off, on the one architecture that most wants it, an optimisation that exists for exactly this class of card.

Set PREBUILD_KERNELS to pin a level for every target.

docs.title: The layer cache is scoped by architecture
docs.text: Covered in Caching. Short version: CACHE_ARCH keeps each architecture's registry cache separate, because before it existed alternating architectures cost two cold builds every time. pytorch-base and triton-wheel stay on the shared ref deliberately — neither compiles device code.

docs.title: Per-architecture pip index
docs.text:
Every wheel here has an architecture-independent filename. torch is torch-2.14.1a0+git5c48869-cp314-cp314-linux_x86_64.whl whether it was built for gfx950 or gfx1201, and amd_aiter-0.1.27 is 131 MB for one architecture and 481 MB for the other. In one directory they overwrite each other and --find-links serves whichever landed last. So the architecture lives in the path.

make wheel-index                  # fetch per arch, generate the indexes
make wheel-index-check            # install each one into a throwaway venv
python3 -m http.server 8081 --directory dist

pip install \
  --index-url http://<host>:8081/index/gfx950/ \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple \
  "rocm-torch[device-gfx950]"

rocm-torch is a metapackage generated per index by .builders/wheelindex.py; its device-<arch> extra pins every wheel in that index at once. Each index declares only its own architecture's extra, so asking gfx950's index for [device-gfx1201] fails rather than installing mismatched binaries. make zot-wheels prints the extra beside each published tag.

Wheels are fetched by architecture-specific tag, never :latest — :latest is written by whichever architecture was pushed last and the wheels inside cannot be told apart afterwards, which is the entire failure this index exists to prevent. The tags come from bake --print rather than being rebuilt in the Makefile, because rocm-bake.hcl owns tag construction and a second copy is exactly the drift check-defaults.py exists to catch.

--extra-index-url is not optional

--index-url replaces PyPI outright, and the first ordinary dependency — numpy, via triton-kernels — then fails to resolve. download.pytorch.org has the same property and the same workaround.

docs.title: Why device-<arch> and not a variant
docs.text:
This is the shape TheRock ships ROCm in — pip install "rocm[device-gfx1153]" — rather than the WheelNext variant mechanism. Variants (PEP 817/825) are the better long-term answer and AMD ships an amd-variant-provider plugin, but both PEPs are Draft, installer support is prototype-only forks of pip and uv, and the published provider matches PyTorch 2.9 on ROCm 6.3/6.4 against a gfx list that does not include gfx950. None of that resolves this stack today.

The extra is spelled device-<arch> so that when variants do land the architecture is already a first-class coordinate, and only the selection mechanism has to change.

CI builds two architectures' indexes on every pull request and asserts that each installs its own and only its own.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Two builds of the same commit must produce the same image digest. Not for its own sake — because the digest is what every downstream FROM pins, and a digest that moves invalidates the entire chain below it.

Three mechanisms get there, and each one was added after the absence of it cost a full rebuild.

docs.title: SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH
docs.text:
BUILD_DATE only reaches the created label. The image config has a created field of its own, which BuildKit stamps with nanosecond wall-clock time regardless. So two builds of identical content produced different config digests, different manifest digests, and every downstream FROM missed. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is what pins that field.

It is set per image, not per repository, and it is a constant:

variable "SDE_EPOCH" { default = "1700000000" }

Two earlier designs failed, and the reasons are worth keeping.

Taking it from HEAD gave the base a new created on every commit, hence a new digest, hence a full downstream rebuild — even for a commit that only touched the Makefile. Measured: Dockerfile.base unchanged between two commits, yet the base digest moved 91db3c2e → aa52684f and nothing downstream could hit.

Taking it from git log -1 --format=%ct -- Dockerfile.<image> used commit history as a proxy for "this image's inputs changed". The proxy does not hold. Squashing 26 commits into 3 made every remaining commit touch every Dockerfile, so all five values collapsed to one timestamp and every image's cache was invalidated at once. Any rebase, squash or filter-branch does this.

Content is what should decide, and content already does — it decides the layer digests. The config created field carries no information anyone reads; the real build date lives in org.opencontainers.image.created. So pinning it to a constant costs nothing and is immune to history being rewritten.

Bump SDE_EPOCH only to force every image to a new digest deliberately. Per-image overrides exist for pinning one without the others:

SDE_PYTORCH=1700000001 make build-pytorch
make build-pytorch BAKE_EXTRA='--set pytorch.args.SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=…'

SDE_BASE, SDE_PYTORCH, SDE_TRITON, SDE_AITER, SDE_RUNTIME, SDE_NIXL, SDE_VLLM, SDE_LMCACHE and SDE_CUPY all default to empty, meaning "use SDE_EPOCH". They are read by bake from the environment, so SDE_PYTORCH=… make … works and make … SDE_PYTORCH=… does not.

docs.title: Provenance attestations
docs.text:
Provenance attestations record build timestamps, so they differ on every build even when the image is byte-identical. Because the attestation shares an OCI index with the image manifest, that changes the digest a downstream FROM pins, and every layer below it misses.

Measured: two identical base builds produced indexes fd260117 and 9c5e5112 wrapped around one unchanged image manifest 91db3c2e. A probe RUN missed the cache across those two indexes, while the same digest under a different tag hit.

So provenance is disabled on every image that is a parent or a named context — pytorch-base, pytorch, triton-wheel, and pytorch-wheel by inheritance:

NO_PROVENANCE = ["type=provenance,disabled=true"]

pytorch-run, aiter-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm and lmcache keep theirs. Nothing builds FROM them, so their digests may churn freely.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
Labels live in the image config, so a changing revision or created gives an image a new digest even when its content is identical. The same trap as SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, arriving by a different route.

Everything that ships gets full OCI provenance:

OCI_LABELS = {
  "org.opencontainers.image.source"   = SOURCE_URL
  "org.opencontainers.image.revision" = VCS_REF
  "org.opencontainers.image.created"  = BUILD_DATE
}

pytorch-base gets identity only:

BASE_LABELS = {
  "org.opencontainers.image.source" = SOURCE_URL
}

Without that, a changing revision would give the base a new digest on every commit, and every downstream FROM would invalidate — re-cloning PyTorch's submodule tree and re-running pip each time. Provenance belongs on the artifacts that ship; the base is an intermediate and should stay content-addressed.

docs.title: VCS_REF and dirty trees
docs.text:
VCS_REF is the short commit hash, with a -dirty suffix appended when the tree has uncommitted changes, so an image built from edited sources can never be mistaken for the commit it came from. It also drives an extra immutable tag on every target:

…/pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950-g<sha>

BUILD_DATE is the commit's own timestamp, not "now", for the same reason SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is pinned.

docs.title: Checking it still holds
docs.text: The warm benchmark scenario exists entirely as a standing check on this. Under the current design a new commit should cost nothing, so warm should build exactly what hot builds. The result is the assertion rather than the number: if warm ever diverges from hot, some per-commit value has found its way back into an image digest. That has happened twice.

docs.title: Serving stack
docs.text:
vLLM, LMCache and NIXL, built from source against this repository's torch rather than installed from published wheels.

They have to be. Their native extensions link against torch's C++ ABI, so a wheel built for AMD's ROCm 7.x torch and one built here cannot share a process — the same constraint that forces AITER to be built here.

docs.title: What gets built
docs.text:
Target What it is nixl-wheel NIXL plus UCX, compiled from source with --with-rocm cupy-wheel CuPy for ROCm; LMCache's MP server imports it at module scope vllm / vllm-wheel The serving image and its wheel lmcache / lmcache-wheel The multi-process cache runtime and its wheel 
make push-serving              # nixl + cupy + vllm + lmcache, built and pushed
make build-vllm                # just vLLM, single builder, no push
make build-lmcache             # just LMCache
make fetch-nixl-wheel          # pull a wheel artifact into ./dist

Refs are overridable per invocation and default to the latest release of each:

make push-serving VLLM_REF=v0.31.0 NIXL_REF=v1.5.0

All four refs are release tags, never branches. A moving ref would be served from the layer cache indefinitely once built, so an "update" would silently be a no-op.

docs.title: NIXL bundles its own UCX
docs.text: Ubuntu's libucx is compiled without ROCm memory-type support, so without a source build every device-memory transfer bounces through host staging. docker/Dockerfile.nixl compiles UCX with --with-rocm and auditwheel bundles it, so installing the wheel is all a consumer needs. NIXL is built once and consumed by both vLLM and LMCache.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
serving/docker-compose.yml runs vLLM and the LMCache MP server as a pair over DOCKER_HOST=ssh://$GPU_HOST, so the file stays here under version control while the engine runs on the machine with the GPU.

make serve-stack               # vLLM + LMCache MP
make serve-vllm                # vLLM alone — the no-offload baseline
make serve-wait                # block until /health answers
make serve-test                # prove the cache is actually working
make serve-test-baseline       # the same, for a serve-vllm stack
make serve-test-l2             # prove the disk tier serves blocks
make serve-logs                # both containers, merged, live
make serve-logs-cache          # the same, filtered to hit/miss/store
make serve-logs-sorted         # a snapshot merged in timestamp order
make serve-status              # what is running on GPU_HOST
make serve-down                # stop and remove

The compose file owns the runtime defaults the way rocm-bake.hcl owns the build ones, and the Makefile reads ${NAME:-default} out of it rather than keeping a second copy. make list-vars prints them with their source marked (compose).

Variable Default What it does KV_TIER cpu cpu = L1 only, file = L1 plus an L2 on disk TRANSFER_MODE lmcache_driven auto, engine_driven or lmcache_driven HSA_IPC_LEGACY 1 Required for cross-container HIP IPC VLLM_DEV_MODE 0 1 exposes /reset_prefix_cache, which serve-test needs L1_SIZE_GB 8 LMCache's host-RAM tier CHUNK_SIZE 256 Tokens per cached chunk MAX_MODEL_LEN 8192 GPU_UTIL 0.90 SERVE_MODEL Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct VLLM_BIND 0.0.0.0 from the Makefile, 127.0.0.1 in the compose file

A variable is passed only when actually set. An exported empty variable is still set, so VAR= would override the compose file's own default with ""; $(if …) omits it instead.

VLLM_BIND differs deliberately. The compose file's 127.0.0.1 is right for someone running it locally; driving it from another machine needs the port off loopback. Narrow it again, or tunnel, if the host is not on a trusted network.

HSA_ENABLE_IPC_MODE_LEGACY decides whether this works at all

It governs whether the two containers can share KV memory. When it is wrong the stack fails at startup, and no amount of TRANSFER_MODE tuning will fix it.

docs.title: The tags come from the GPU host
docs.text:
SERVE_ARCH asks GPU_HOST which GPU it has, via rocminfo over SSH, the same way GPU_RENDER_GID asks it for the render group. The build default is gfx950 while the serving host here is a gfx1201 RX 9070 XT, and deriving the serving tag from the build architecture asked Zot for an image nobody had built — the only symptom being a pull failure naming a plausible-looking tag.

It falls back to the build architecture when the host is unreachable or has no rocminfo, which is the right answer when someone is driving this against a single machine.

docs.title: /health is not evidence
docs.text:
LMCache on ROCm has a failure mode where the endpoint serves every request correctly and caches nothing. In LMCache#4419 a reporter ran eight days at a zero hit rate with no error anywhere.

make serve-test sends the same long prefix twice, requires the second prefill to be measurably cheaper, and then reads LMCache's own log for the store and the retrieve — because vLLM's own prefix caching can make the timing alone look fine.

serve-test-l2 goes further: it empties LMCache's L1 as well as vLLM's VRAM between the two requests, so a hit can only have come off disk. It needs KV_TIER=file.

make serve-logs merges both containers' streams tagged by container, rather than using compose logs. The useful lines alternate — vLLM says what it asked for, LMCache says whether it had it — and reading them apart hid a failure once already: LMCache died on a missing CuPy and vLLM spent five minutes waiting before reporting a generic engine error.

docs.title: Running the images directly
docs.text:
# vLLM. AITER is installed but off by default.
docker run --rm --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri -p 8000:8000 \
    -e VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 \
    snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/vllm:latest \
    serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B

# LMCache's multi-process deployment: a controller holding the
# cluster-wide index, and one or more cache servers holding the blocks.
# The image has no default role — name the CLI you want.
docker run --rm -p 9000:9000 \
    snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/lmcache:latest \
    lmcache_controller --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9000

docker run --rm --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri -p 8100:8100 \
    snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/lmcache:latest \
    lmcache_server 0.0.0.0 8100 cpu

The two LMCache CLIs take arguments differently

lmcache_controller takes flags. lmcache_server takes three positional arguments — host, port, storage. Giving the server flags makes it print a usage line and exit 1.

docs.title: Three upstream constraints
docs.text:
LMCache declares requires-python >=3.10,<3.14. This lane is cp314, because Ubuntu 26.04 — the only base AMD publishes ROCm 10.1 for — ships no other Python. The wheel is installed with --ignore-requires-python; the extension is compiled here against this interpreter, so the ABI matches by construction. Revisit when upstream raises the bound.

Both projects' requirement files carry CUDA-only or x86-wheel-only pins — cufile-python, nvtx, tilelang, amd-quark, mooncake-transfer-engine-rocm and others. These are stripped before the build, which also keeps them out of the wheel's install_requires. The lists are build args, VLLM_DROP_REQS and LMCACHE_DROP_REQS, so a dependency can be let back in once it has a usable wheel.

torchvision is a CUDA wheel in these images, and that is not fixed here. /etc/pip-constraints.txt pins torch and triton to the ROCm builds, but there is no ROCm torchvision in this pipeline — it is resolved from PyPI by docker/Dockerfile.pytorch's optional-extras step, and vLLM's requirements/rocm.txt keeps it reachable through timm. Its _C_stable.so links libtorch_cuda and libc10_cuda, so import torchvision fails at load time. Nothing in the text-model serving path touches it, which is why the build and the import checks stay green — but vision and video models will fail at serve time until a ROCm torchvision is built the way torch and triton are.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: Day-to-day running of the fleet.

docs.title: Routine
docs.text:
make push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool    # build and publish everything, scheduled
make watch                         # follow it from a second terminal
make layer-summary                 # how much of each image was rebuilt
make cache-summary                 # is the compiler cache taking objects?

push-all with the pool sentinel is the usual way to build. Everything else is diagnosis.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
make zot-check        # registry active and answering
make cache-check      # every node can reach the compiler cache
make builder-health   # which builders can take work
make builder-status   # all builders and their nodes
make builder-load     # CPU, cores and load per node
make version-check    # are any upstream pins behind?

builder-health is what builder-ensure gates every build target on, so a build against a dead node fails fast rather than hanging. It reports running, inactive or error per node.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Four workflows, all on GitHub-hosted runners. None of them builds a real image — the images need this fleet — so CI validates structure and agreement rather than output.

CI — Dockerfile & bake validation runs on pull requests and pushes to main, path-filtered to the build files. It enumerates the bake targets out of rocm-bake.hcl into a matrix and, for each one, checks that bake --print resolves, that the Dockerfile it names exists, and that its cache ref and its tags agree about the architecture. It also builds two architectures' pip indexes and asserts each installs its own and only its own, runs check-defaults.py, validates the serving compose file and that the services the Makefile drives still exist, and HCL-lints the bake file.

Lint & spelling runs codespell, shellcheck at -S warning, hadolint over docker/Dockerfile.*, actionlint and yamllint over .github/, and ruff --select E,F plus py_compile over every tracked Python file. It also runs make version-scrub-check, which fails if the generated version tables in README.md and the docs have drifted from rocm-bake.hcl. That gate lives here rather than in ci.yml because ci.yml is path-filtered to the build files — README.md and docs/ are not in that list, so a pull request that hand-edited the table would have run no job at all.

ci.yml also renders a synthetic perf report and asserts every SVG is well-formed, that timeline spans do not overlap, that labels fit their bars, and that a partial run degrades rather than crashes — then runs check-contracts.py over the producer/parser pairs.

Build & push — ROCm PyTorch is workflow_dispatch only.

Version check — upstream releases runs Mondays. It runs .builders/versioncheck.py --markdown --no-zot — the same script make version-check runs here, so the weekly report and the one an operator runs cannot disagree — and opens or comments on a single tracking issue when a pin is behind upstream. The published-wheels column is skipped there: the registry is a tailnet name a GitHub runner cannot resolve, and an empty column would read as "we have published nothing".

Docs builds this site and deploys it to the gh-pages branch on every push to main that touches docs/ or mkdocs.yml. It preserves the data/ directory already on that branch, because that is where the published benchmark results live and they are written from a build node, not from CI.

docs.title: Cleaning up
docs.text:
make clean         # built images, locally, for every arch in ARCHES
make clean-cache   # cache images, locally
docker system df   # what is using the disk
docker system prune -a

Both clean targets are local only. The registry has to be pruned separately, and clean-cache covers only four of the ten cache repositories.

docker buildx prune is fleet-shared

These builders are shared with another project. Pruning a node's BuildKit store empties its layers too. The frozen benchmark scenario does this deliberately, which is why it is not in the nightly rotation.

docs.title: When something is wrong
docs.text: Troubleshooting covers the failures that have actually happened on this fleet, with the log line that identifies each one.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Failures that have actually happened here, with the line that identifies each one.

docs.title: Connection refused
docs.text:
systemctl status zot              # bare metal, not a container
sudo journalctl -u zot -n 50
curl -s http://snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/v2/_catalog
make zot-check

docs.title: Two failures that look similar from a build log
docs.text:
Log line Cause no such host The builder cannot resolve the tailnet name. It was created without --driver-opt network=host, so Docker gave it the upstream resolver instead of the host's MagicDNS one. http: server gave HTTP response to HTTPS client DNS is fine but the client will not speak plain HTTP. For the Docker daemon, check insecure-registries in /etc/docker/daemon.json; for BuildKit, confirm the builder was created with --config .builders/buildkitd-strix.toml.

Both settings are fixed at builder-create time, so the fix is always docker buildx rm <name> then make builder-<name>. Editing the toml does nothing to an existing builder. Inspect with docker buildx inspect <name>.

If pushes get 401: docker login snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080 -u ci.

docs.title: Push dies at exactly 60 seconds
docs.text:
Zot's default HTTP read timeout is 60 s, measured across the whole request body. The ROCm base image has a single 8.67 GB layer, which cannot cross a 1 Gb/s link in under ~73 s, so every push of it failed at the 60 s mark: Zot discarded the partial upload and returned 500, and BuildKit retried with backoff.

The client-side error is a connection reset, which reads like a network fault rather than a timeout. The giveaway is Zot's own log:

PUT /v2/.../blobs/uploads/...  statusCode: 500  latency: "1m0s"
error: "read tcp ...: i/o timeout"   Content-Length: 8672333352

/etc/zot/config.json needs:

"http": {
  "readTimeout": "30m",
  "writeTimeout": "30m"
}

then sudo systemctl restart zot. That layer then pushes in ~200 s.

Zot is deployed from outside this repository, so the setting belongs in whatever provisions it, or it reverts on the next deploy.

docs.title: The compiler cache
docs.text:
The build refuses to start when the store is unreachable, so a silent no-cache build should not happen. If it does:

make cache-summary    # endpoint, size, disk, deltas and hit rates
make cache-check      # can every node reach it?
make cache-logs       # the WebDAV access log

Run cache-summary twice a minute apart during a build: the interval line is the one that matters. The store itself cannot report a hit rate — WebDAV has no stats verb — so that column is read back out of the telemetry textfile, per target, from the last build of each.

docs.title: Three failure modes with distinct signatures
docs.text:
Log line Cause No such file or directory on a source path The client reached a server outside its own container. Structurally impossible now that the server is addressed over a unix socket, but this is what it looked like. cache storage failed to read … I/O error The store's address did not resolve. Check the [dns] block in .builders/buildkitd-strix.toml, and that the Makefile resolved WEBDAV_IP — build containers address the store by IP, not by name. Cache write errors climbing The store's filesystem is full. make cache-summary shows the disk line.

SCCACHE_LOG=debug reveals what sccache's "Cache errors" counter is actually counting; it is not the default because debug logs every lookup, and a cold Triton does 361 of them.

Builder settings are fixed at create time, so after changing the buildkitd config:

docker buildx rm snoc-strix && make builder-snoc-strix

docs.title: "HIP not found"
docs.text:
rocm-smi --showversion     # are the ROCm modules loaded?
ls -la /dev/kfd /dev/dri   # is the GPU visible?

Note that compiling for an architecture does not need a GPU. This matters only for make test and make gpu-test.

docs.title: A build fails at the last target, every time
docs.text: If pytorch-test has found its way into a group: it cannot run inside the build graph at all. Its stage exits 1 when torch.cuda.is_available() is false, and a BuildKit RUN step has no /dev/kfd. Use make test on a GPU node instead.

docs.title: AITER's wheel build exits 1 after ~51 minutes
docs.text: On RDNA. Every kernel compiles and the build then fails in the JIT module phase: six of 68 modules carry CDNA-only code and setup.py treats a failed module as fatal. The build should have selected PREBUILD_LEVEL=0 — check that PREBUILD_KERNELS has not been pinned to 2 in the environment. See Multiple GFX targets.

docs.title: A build is wedged
docs.text:
make build-stop        # cancel builds started from this repo
make builder-restart   # restart buildkitd on $(BUILDER)

builder-restart drops that node's in-memory build state. The registry layer cache and the shared compiler cache are untouched, so the next build still picks up where it can.

A build cancelled by build-stop is recorded by BuildKit as status Error with no detail, which is indistinguishable from a real failure. make watch reads a stop file so it can label those correctly rather than showing a red "error" for something you stopped on purpose.

docs.title: Alternating architectures are both always cold
docs.text: Fixed by CACHE_ARCH, but if it recurs: check that the target in question actually scopes its cache ref by architecture. pytorch-base and triton-wheel deliberately do not, because neither compiles device code.

docs.title: Insufficient disk space
docs.text:
docker system df
docker system prune -a

Remember the BuildKit store is bounded by gckeepstorage = "100GB" per node and is shared with the other project on these builders.

docs.title: No metrics appeared
docs.text:
./telemetry/build.sh --builder snoc-strix pytorch   # run it directly
docker buildx history ls --builder snoc-strix       # is there history to read?

Metrics land in telemetry/out/ instead of the node_exporter directory when that directory is not writable — the wrapper says so when it falls back.

sccache counters are absent when a target was fully layer-cached: the build step never ran, so it printed no stats. That is correct.

docs.title: A frozen run is recorded as frozen*
docs.text: The registry eviction was refused, so the run was really a cold run. Zot needs deletes enabled. Such rows are excluded from every published ratio rather than averaged in.

docs.title: The harness exits immediately saying a build is running
docs.text: By design — two builds on one node contend for cores and memory, and every timing would be meaningless. It exits 0 so it is safe to drive from cron. make build-status shows what is running.

docs.title: Results look implausible
docs.text: Check the job count. The same cold PyTorch is 6892 s at 5 jobs and 2342 s at 32, and the harness only prints a ratio when both sides were measured at the same width. BENCH_MAX_JOBS pins it. See Methodology.

docs.title: The endpoint is healthy but nothing is cached
docs.text: /health is not evidence. Run make serve-test, which requires the second prefill of a repeated prefix to be measurably cheaper and reads LMCache's own log for the store and the retrieve.

docs.title: The stack fails at startup
docs.text: Check HSA_ENABLE_IPC_MODE_LEGACY. It decides whether the two containers can share KV memory at all, and no amount of TRANSFER_MODE tuning will work around it.

docs.title: A pull fails naming a plausible-looking tag
docs.text: The serving tag comes from GPU_HOST's own architecture, not the build default. make list-vars prints the resolved SERVE_ARCH, VLLM_TAG and LMCACHE_TAG. If the host is unreachable, SERVE_ARCH falls back to the build architecture — which may well be an image nobody has built.

docs.title: import torchvision fails
docs.text: Known and not fixed here. torchvision is a CUDA wheel in these images; nothing in the text-model serving path touches it, but vision and video models will fail at serve time. See Serving stack.

docs.title: Everything is slow and nothing is obviously broken
docs.text:
In order:

  1. make builder-logs — a registry, DNS or cache fault shows up in the daemon's log while the build itself merely looks slow.
  2. make cache-summary — twice, a minute apart. If the object count is not moving during a compile, the compiler cache is not being written.
  3. make layer-summary — a target that moved nodes cannot use the previous node's local BuildKit cache and must refetch from the registry.
  4. make builder-load — something else may be on the node.

docs.title: Build performance
docs.text:
Two harnesses, answering different questions.

This page is bench.sh: one target at a time, four cache conditions, an isolated compiler cache. It answers what does this target cost, and its numbers are comparable run to run.

Instrumented fleet runs is make perf-run: every wheel at once, across all three nodes, with CPU, cache and registry traffic sampled throughout. It answers what does a full cold build look like, and its numbers are throughput under contention.

Do not quote a number from one as if it came from the other.

docs.title: The four cache conditions
docs.text:
Measured rather than estimated. They nest: each one is the one below it with a further cache taken away.

flowchart LR
    frozen["<b>frozen</b><br/>nothing, anywhere"] --> cold["<b>cold</b><br/>base image local"]
    cold --> warm["<b>warm</b><br/>caches populated,<br/>new commit"]
    warm --> hot["<b>hot</b><br/>same commit,<br/>everything cached"]

docs.title: frozen
docs.text:
Cold, and Zot holds no pull-through copy of the upstream base image either, so its layers egress from Docker Hub.

What a brand-new site costs, before any of this fleet's infrastructure has warmed up. The ROCm base is a single 8.67 GB layer, so the difference between frozen and cold is essentially WAN bandwidth — and it is the number to quote when someone asks what the local registry is worth.

make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=frozen BUILDER=snoc-think

frozen is destructive and is not in the nightly rotation

It deletes Zot's cached manifest for the upstream base, and it runs docker buildx prune -af on the target node — which empties that node's BuildKit content store, including any other project's layers. These builders are shared. BENCH_FROZEN_PRUNE=0 skips the prune, at the cost of only re-pulling whatever BuildKit happened to drop.

If Zot refuses the delete, the run is recorded with registry_evicted: "partial" and shown as frozen*. It is a cold run wearing a frozen label, and it is excluded from every published ratio rather than averaged in — counting it would quietly drive the registry's apparent value towards nothing.

docs.title: cold
docs.text:
No layer cache, no compiler cache, but the base image is resident in Zot. What a new build node, or a changed base image, costs. The upper bound on compile cost.

--no-cache alone is not cold: sccache would still serve every object from the shared store and the build would finish in minutes while measuring nothing. The harness also sets FORCE_RECACHE and isolates the run under its own SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX.

make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=cold
make cold-build COLD_TARGET=pytorch   # the same conditions, outside the harness

docs.title: warm
docs.text:
Layer and compiler caches are populated, but SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH moved — which is what every new commit does, including commits that touch nothing the image depends on. The case that matters day to day.

Under the current design that costs nothing, and the result is the assertion rather than the number: warm builds exactly what hot builds, so if warm ever diverges from hot, some per-commit value has found its way back into an image digest. That has happened twice — once when the epoch came from HEAD's timestamp, and once when a squash collapsed the per-image timestamps. See Reproducibility.

docs.title: hot
docs.text:
Same commit, everything cached. The lower bound, and mostly a check that the caches are being read at all.

Note that the harness distinguishes two kinds of hot run when it computes ratios: one where the compile step ran and sccache served every object, and one where BuildKit skipped the step outright. They answer different questions and are reported separately.

docs.title: Measured results
docs.text:
Medians, keyed by target, builder, architecture and job count. Both architecture and job count are in the key because both are dominant variables rather than nuisance ones: the same cold PyTorch is 6892 s at 5 jobs and 2342 s at 32, and vLLM's kernel prebuild is about 50 minutes on gfx950 against hours on gfx1201 — AITER drops to PREBUILD_KERNELS=0 on RDNA entirely. Cold on one architecture over hot on another is not a ratio. See Methodology.

PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH=gfx1201 make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=cold measures that architecture; the harness resolves the value through make, so it is always the one a real build would have used.

docs.title: Every run
docs.text: Each point is one build. The spread is real and large — PyTorch's hot time varies about threefold run to run — which is why the tables above quote medians and print n beside them.

docs.title: Reproducing this
docs.text:
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=cold BUILDER=snoc-think   # one scenario
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=all                       # cold, warm, hot
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=everything                # and frozen first
make bench-report                                   # render as markdown

The harness refuses to run while a real build is in flight on the target builder: two builds on one node contend for cores and memory, and every timing would be meaningless. It exits 0 in that case rather than failing, so it is safe to drive from cron.

Results accumulate as JSON lines in /var/tmp/rocm-bench/results.jsonl, one per build, so a partial run is still usable and successive nights add to the record rather than overwriting it.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
The numbers on this page come from a file on the gh-pages branch, not from the repository. Nothing in main carries benchmark data.

make bench-data              # aggregate into dist/bench/bench.json
make bench-publish           # commit it onto gh-pages
make bench-publish PUSH=1    # and push

This runs from a build node because that is the only place the data exists — a GitHub-hosted runner can neither reproduce the builds nor read the results. The docs workflow preserves data/ when it deploys the site, so the two writers do not clobber each other.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: .builders/bench.sh is the harness. It runs one make build-* per measurement, parses the build log, and appends a JSON line. Everything below is a correction to something that produced a wrong number first.

docs.title: What a run records
docs.text:
{
  "ts": "2026-10-20T02:00:00+00:00",
  "scenario": "cold",
  "target": "pytorch",
  "builder": "snoc-think",
  "arch": "gfx950",
  "seconds": 2342,
  "rc": 0,
  "steps_cached": 0,
  "steps_total": 11,
  "sccache_requests": 5674,
  "sccache_hits": 0,
  "sccache_misses": 5674,
  "max_jobs": 10,
  "node_load_at_start": 0.4,
  "node_load_at_end": 12.0,
  "registry_evicted": null,
  "failure": null,
  "log": "/var/tmp/rocm-bench/logs/cold-pytorch-…​.log"
}

A failing build is a result, and recording it is the point — the harness never aborts on one. failure carries the first line that looks like a cause rather than the generic wrapper.

log is stripped before publication, along with nothing else: the json mode emits every other field.

docs.title: Guards before a run
docs.text:
Is the node busy? The harness asks buildx what the builder is actually solving, not the process table. pgrep -f matches a pattern anywhere in a command line — including the command line of whatever invoked the script, and of the check's own subshell — so an earlier version reported busy against itself. It was also fleet-wide: a build on any node blocked a benchmark on an idle one, and these builders are shared with another project.

Has memory settled? MAX_JOBS is derived inside the build from MemAvailable, sampled once when the compile step starts and fixed for the whole build. Launching a benchmark straight after another one samples it while BuildKit is still flushing the previous build's layers: a cold PyTorch started that way derived MAX_JOBS=3 on a 30 GB node that reported 18 GB free two minutes later. Across slots that node has produced 3, 4, 7 and 10 — mostly scheduling artefact, not node. The harness polls until two consecutive readings agree, which keeps the derivation (the thing being exercised) while removing the artefact.

Settling is necessary but not sufficient. The derivation happens when the compile step starts, by which point the build's own earlier steps — fetching the base image, the checkout, aotriton — have taken memory of their own. A cold PyTorch that settled at 21 GB still derived 5, where the same node gives a hot run 10. So cold and hot are measured at different job counts by construction.

BENCH_MAX_JOBS pins it when the point is to compare scenarios. Leave it unset when the point is to exercise the derivation itself.

docs.title: Parsing the log
docs.text: Two numbers come out of the build log, and both were wrong at first in instructive ways.

docs.title: Steps cached
docs.text:
A step here is a vertex BuildKit labels [n/m], and cached means that same vertex reported CACHED. Not the telemetry wrapper's count: that counts loading the Dockerfile, the dockerignore, metadata and exporting among the total — none of which can ever be cached — so a fully-cached base build reports 5/12 while every one of its five actual steps was CACHED.

The vertex name carries a bake-target prefix whenever the build has more than one target, and pytorch always does now because it pulls triton-wheel in as a named context. BuildKit emits [pytorch builder 4/11] and [triton-wheel builder 9/11] where a single-target build emits a bare [builder 9/11]. An earlier regex allowed only the bare form, so a PyTorch benchmark counted zero steps out of zero.

docs.title: sccache counters
docs.text:
Not from ^Cache hits: the lines carry a BuildKit prefix (#32 178.7 Cache hits 5674), so that anchor never matched and every run recorded 0 hits.

And not from the telemetry summary either, which was the first fix and was also wrong. A PyTorch build prints two stats blocks, its own and Triton's, and the wrapper attributed Triton's numbers to both images: a run whose PyTorch compile reported 5674 hits was summarised as 361 hits, which is Triton's figure.

BuildKit does carry the association, in the step number. The vertex header #32 [pytorch builder 10/11] RUN … ties step 32 to pytorch, and every stats line from that step is prefixed #32. Mapping headers to targets and then selecting that target's steps is exact, with no heuristic about ordering or magnitude.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
frozen and cold runs set SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX to a per-run value, so they never pollute or evict the fleet's shared compiler cache. The prefix is a directory in the WebDAV store and is deleted immediately after the run — a cold run writes the whole compile output and these add up fast.

cache-to is cleared for every benchmark run. The Docker credential helper on this host fails with gpg: public key decryption failed outside an interactive session, so registry writes are impossible unattended. Reads are anonymous and still work, so cache hits are measured faithfully; what these numbers exclude is push time, which is not what is being timed.

docs.title: Forcing a recompile
docs.text:
Until recently the only way to make a hot build actually compile was to give MAX_JOBS a value it had not had before, since changing a build arg changes the layer key. That conflated the cache-buster with the variable under test: each job count was usable exactly once per tree state.

BENCH_FORCE_COMPILE=1 instead writes an HCL override setting no-cache-filter = ["builder"], which asks BuildKit to ignore cache for one stage and nothing else, so the same width can be measured repeatedly. It has to arrive as an override file — bake accepts the attribute there, but --set target.no-cache-filter= is silently dropped (tested on buildx 0.30.1; it does not appear in --print).

Note it invalidates every step in the stage, not just the compile: the git clone, the sccache download and the pip installs all re-run.

Whether it changes the timing enough to matter is not established. It looked that way from two samples — 403 s and 429 s against a 267 s pin-change run — but with every converged run counted, the pin-change method spans 203–617 s and contains the forced range entirely. PyTorch's hot time varies about threefold run to run whatever forces the compile, and that swamps any method effect this data could show. Treat the two as interchangeable until something separates them.

docs.title: How the ratios are computed
docs.text:
Three pools, keyed by (target, builder, arch, max_jobs):

Pool Which rows frozen scenario == "frozen" and the registry eviction succeeded cold scenario == "cold" compiled scenario == "hot" where under half the steps were cached skipped scenario == "hot" where at least half were cached

and three ratios:

  • registry — frozen ÷ cold. What Zot's pull-through is worth.
  • compiler cache — cold ÷ compiled. sccache served the requests instead of the compiler.
  • layer cache — compiled ÷ skipped. BuildKit skipped the compile step outright, so sccache saw no requests at all.

Dividing cold by whichever hot run came last conflated the last two and once printed "2297.3x" — a cold run against a 3 s layer-cache hit that compiled nothing.

Whether the compile ran is judged on steps cached rather than on sccache having reported anything. Rows written before the sccache parser was fixed carry requests=0 because nothing was recorded, not because nothing was compiled; two Triton rows at 529 s and 218 s have requests=0 and steps 0/3, so they plainly compiled, and counting them as layer-cache hits produced "layer cache a further 0x".

docs.title: Which sample
docs.text:
The markdown report quotes the most recent run at a key, not the best and not the median. Each of the others was tried and each is wrong here.

The minimum picks an outlier, and picking it on both sides biases the ratio in opposite directions: cold runs vary far more than hot ones, so min(cold) picks a sample that shrinks the ratio while min(hot) picks one that inflates it.

The median assumes the samples are drawn from one population, and they are not — this pipeline changed underneath its own measurements. The compiler cache converged partway through, and rows written before the sccache parser was fixed record no hit data at all. Averaging a run from before a fix with one from after describes a system that never existed.

The question a ratio answers is what the cache buys now, so the newest sample is the right estimator, and n with the observed range is printed beside it so the spread stays visible.

The charts on the results page use medians instead, and deliberately. A chart is showing a distribution over time; there the newest point belongs in the series, not in the summary.

docs.title: Why job count and architecture are in the key
docs.text:
Both are dominant parameters, not nuisance ones.

The same cold PyTorch is 6892 s at 5 jobs and 2342 s at 32. An earlier version pooled runs across widths and reported "pytorch hot, n=12, 244–1366s", which spans pins 5 to 15 plus runs taken before the compiler cache had converged. No average over that means anything.

Architecture is the same mistake in a different coordinate. vLLM's kernel prebuild is about 50 minutes on gfx950 and hours on gfx1201, and AITER drops to PREBUILD_KERNELS=0 on RDNA entirely — so cold on one architecture divided by hot on another is not a ratio either.

The harness resolves the architecture through make rather than defaulting to a literal, so it is exactly what a real build would use and gfx950 is not duplicated out of rocm-bake.hcl. Rows written before the field existed are read as gfx950: the harness never set PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH then, so they used the bake default, which has been gfx950 since before the oldest result on file.

A ratio is printed only when cold and hot were measured at the same width and architecture. Anything measured at one only is still shown, just not as a ratio.

docs.title: Contamination
docs.text: The builders are shared with another project, and a concurrent build skewed the first timings taken here. The node's one-minute load average is recorded at the start and at the end, because one sample at t=0 does not characterise a run lasting ten to twenty minutes: the slowest cold Triton on record, 1168 s against a 432–669 s cluster, began at load 0.99 — the lowest of its group — and the node's fifteen-minute average reached 41 on 32 cores by the time it finished. Contention arriving after the start was invisible, and it is the best candidate for the spread these numbers carry.

docs.title: Instrumented fleet runs
