docs.text: Every wheel built across the whole fleet at once, with CPU, memory, compiler-cache and registry traffic sampled throughout, and a report that explains where the time went.

docs.title: Three harnesses, three questions
docs.text:
bench.sh make perf-run make perf-build runs targets one at a time across the fleet at once across the fleet at once caches isolated cold: none both, as normal answers what does this target cost what does a full cold build look like what does a build I would actually run look like numbers are isolated per-target throughput under contention throughput under contention

Do not quote a number from one as if it came from another

bench.sh serialises on purpose and isolates its compiler cache, so its per-target times are comparable run to run. The two perf-* harnesses run the fleet flat out, so three builds share the sccache store and the registry — both of which live on Strix, which is also a build node.

perf-build is the same instrumentation on an ordinary build: layer cache and sccache both live, results pushed, the fleet's real sccache prefix. It is the one to use when the question is about the build you actually run rather than about a build from nothing — and the two differ more than you would expect, because a warm build's cost is almost entirely export rather than compute.

docs.title: Running one
docs.text:
make perf-plan                      # placement only, builds nothing
make perf-run PERF_ARCH=gfx1201     # cold: no caches, hours
make perf-build PERF_ARCH=gfx1201   # normal: caches on, pushes
make perf-report                    # markdown + SVG from the newest run
make perf-serve                     # live chart on :8090
make perf-runs                      # list collected runs

Cold here means --no-cache and an sccache prefix of its own — the same isolation bench.sh uses. A cold run must not evict the fleet's working cache, and it must not be allowed to hit it either.

perf-serve binds every interface

Not just the tailnet, because the usual viewer is a laptop on the LAN that is not on tailscale. What that exposes is build telemetry — hostnames, CPU and memory figures, build step names — with no credentials and no registry access. Narrow it with PERF_BIND=<ip>, and stop it when you are done.

It regenerates every 30 s and re-resolves which run is newest each cycle, so it picks up a run that starts after the server did.

docs.title: What a run collects
docs.text:
Into /var/tmp/rocm-perf/<stamp>/, each from the cheapest source that actually answers its question rather than from one general-purpose collector:

File From Answers samples.jsonl node_exporter on all three nodes, polled CPU, memory, disk and network over time trace-<target>.json the builder's own build record what ran, when, for how long sccache.log the WebDAV vhost's nginx log, sliced to this run what was written to the compiler cache, with sizes zot.jsonl Zot's structured log, sliced to this run layer-cache and image writes, with sizes artifacts.txt wheelhouse.py what ended up published index.html + data.json perfreport.py the interactive chart, and the sidecar it polls

make perf-report writes report.md with SVG charts beside it, plus index.html for interrogating a run: overlaid CPU and memory lines, a clickable legend that filters by builder and by target, and per-band hover showing the actual RUN commands a phase covers.

CPU and memory share one axis because both are percentages. A second y-scale would make it a dual-axis chart, which is the chart form that misleads most reliably; memory is distinguished by dash instead, so colour keeps following the builder.

perf-serve polls data.json rather than reloading, because the legend is the filter: a reload would discard whichever builders and targets the viewer had narrowed to, which is exactly the state someone mid-question is in.

docs.title: build and total are different numbers
docs.text:
The per-target table carries both. build is the span of the target's own steps; total is what the builder reported for the whole record. The gap is setup plus export, and it is usually the larger of the two.

Transfers never widen the build column — that column exists to exclude them. If the two disagree by minutes, the difference is the export, and on a warm build it is nearly all of it.

docs.title: Cache export is not build time — in cold mode
docs.text:
--no-push suppresses the image push but not the cache export, which is a separate registry write. In cold mode perfrun.sh clears it with --set *.cache-to=, as bench.sh does, because the cost is not small:

On one gfx1201 run triton-wheel reported 38m52s, of which the trace accounted for 15m48s. The other 23m04s — 59% of its headline duration — was uploading mode=max cache.

A harness measuring a build from nothing must not also time its own uploads.

docs.title: In normal mode the export is the point
docs.text:
make perf-build reports the upload rather than suppressing it. perftrace.py keeps BuildKit's HTTP PUT/POST spans alongside the step spans, so the chart bands them as upload and the hover names the blob and its size.

Those spans were discarded until a triton-wheel run showed 92 s of steps inside a 430 s record, with the missing 336 s invisible: a node that looked idle for most of its build was in fact uploading 6.4 GB.

docs.title: Dependency ordering, not stage barriers
docs.text:
Perf runs schedule from the bake graph. A target starts when every dependency inside the run has finished and been pushed, and not before; everything else it needs is resolved from Zot and checked by preflight before any build begins.

This replaced two earlier modes, and it is worth knowing why both failed.

Stage barriers ordered work correctly but idled whole nodes waiting on unrelated targets:

On one gfx1201 run stage 1 took 44m16s of wall clock to do 77m09s of work, leaving 55m39s of idle builder time, with the weakest node idle for 82% of it.

Flat per-node queues dropped the barrier and recovered that time, but could not express a dependency at all. That was safe only while every wheel was self-contained — and stopped being true the moment a run included a target that builds FROM another, which is how a gfx1250 run scheduled vllm-wheel against a pytorch image nothing was building.

Within the ordering constraint the packing is unchanged: longest-first onto the node that would finish it soonest, one build per node at a time, because several concurrent builds on one box each derive MAX_JOBS from MemAvailable as though they were alone and oversubscribe it.

docs.title: What a perf run measures
docs.text:
PERF_TARGETS defaults to bake's wheels group plus pytorch.

pytorch is not a wheel, so the group alone omitted it — and it is the most expensive target in the graph as well as the image every other wheel builds FROM. Leaving it out measured the cheap half of a build, and on an arch nobody had built before it scheduled wheels against an image that did not exist.

Including it costs little on a normal run, where the layer cache serves it in seconds. On a cold run it genuinely rebuilds, which is what cold means.

docs.title: What a target costs depends on which node runs it
docs.text:
.builders/target-costs is the input to that packing, and it has two terms because a target's cost is not one number:

build <target> <seconds>   compile cost, roughly node-independent
cache <target> <bytes>     what the target transfers when it exports
netmb <node>   <MB/s>      that node's upload throughput to the store

The cost of running a target on a node is build + cache/netmb, and the packer picks the node that finishes it soonest rather than the one that is least loaded.

The second term is not a refinement. The fleet's upload speeds span a factor of 25 — 3000 MB/s on the store host itself, 90 wired, 3.7 over WiFi — so the same 6.4 GB export is about a minute on one node and about 28 on another.

Ranking on build time alone sent triton-wheel, the largest export of any target, to the only node behind WiFi. Moving it to a wired node took it from 25m25s to 7m09s.

Re-measure after anything that moves the build materially, and re-measure netmb if the fleet is rewired, since that is the term that now dominates.

Take the byte figures from a normal run

A cold run passes --no-push, so its export counts the cache but not the image — which under-counted aiter-wheel by 4.3×.

A stale table degrades the schedule, never the build, and check-contracts.py fails if a wheel or a node is missing from it — because the fallback for a missing entry is to cost it at one second.

docs.title: Warm runs can invert which node is critical
docs.text:
These are cold-build costs. On a warm build every build term collapses towards zero while the cache terms stay:

In one perf-build run pytorch-wheel was a cache hit and freed its node after 55 s, leaving the WiFi node's four small targets — 2.8 GB between them — as the critical path of a 26-minute run.

Queues are fixed at plan time, so nothing migrates once packed.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
Several of those streams are produced by one file and parsed by another, with nothing but a comment connecting them — an nginx log_format and a regex, the balancer's placement line and the report's parser, the sampler's fields and the report's readers, target-costs and the packer.

Every one has the same failure mode: the producer changes, the consumer silently matches nothing, and the report renders perfectly while saying 0 where it should say something.

.builders/check-contracts.py asserts each pair still agrees. It reads files only — no registry, no GPU, no builders, no sudo — so it runs on a bare CI runner in under a second, and ci.yml runs it alongside a synthetic render of a perf report.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Every build records its own metrics. This is separate from the benchmark harness: telemetry runs on every build including real ones, the harness runs deliberately under controlled conditions.

telemetry/build.sh wraps a bake invocation, runs it, then writes Prometheus metrics for each target it produced — and exits with the bake's own status, so it is a drop-in replacement for a bare bake call. The make build-* and make push-* targets already route through it.

./telemetry/build.sh --builder snoc-think pytorch
make build-pytorch                   # the same thing
TELEMETRY=0 make build-pytorch       # a bare bake

Both data sources already exist, so nothing has to be instrumented and no collector daemon runs:

  • BuildKit's history API (docker buildx history inspect) records every build's duration, status, and how many steps came from the layer cache.
  • sccache's own stats, printed at the end of the build step and scraped back out of the replayed build log. They cannot be queried afterwards: the sccache server lives and dies with the build container.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
All eight per-target metrics are gauges, labelled {target="…",builder="…"}:

Metric Meaning rocm_build_duration_seconds BuildKit-reported duration rocm_build_steps_total Steps in the build rocm_build_steps_cached How many came from the layer cache rocm_build_layer_cache_hit_ratio Cached steps over total rocm_build_target_success 1 if the target completed rocm_build_sccache_hits Compiler-cache hits for that build rocm_build_sccache_misses Compiler-cache misses rocm_build_sccache_hit_ratio Hits over hits plus misses

Three more describe the invocation as a whole, labelled {builder="…"}:

Metric Meaning rocm_build_invocation_duration_seconds Wall-clock for the whole bake rocm_build_invocation_success 1 if the bake exited 0 rocm_build_last_run_timestamp_seconds When the invocation finished

A HELP/TYPE block is emitted only when at least one sample exists for that name, so a scrape never sees a declared-but-empty metric.

docs.title: Where it lands
docs.text:
/var/lib/node_exporter/textfile_collector/rocm_pytorch_build.prom

written to a temp path and renamed, so the collector never reads a partial file. node_exporter already runs on :9100 here, so a scrape of that target picks them up with no extra job.

Writing to the collector directory needs permission on it. When that directory is not a writable directory, the wrapper falls back to telemetry/out/ (gitignored) and says so.

docs.title: Attributing sccache stats to a target
docs.text:
The subtle part. Replayed history records carry no bake-target prefix on their vertex headers, so the step cannot be identified the way the benchmark harness does it live. Instead each Dockerfile tees its stats to a known file, and the wrapper finds the vertex whose command contains that marker:

Target Marker pytorch /opt/pytorch/sccache-stats.txt triton-wheel /wheels-triton-sccache-stats.txt aiter-wheel /wheels-aiter-sccache-stats.txt

Having found the step number, it reads that step's stats lines. With no marker present it falls back to the last stats block in the log, which is a guess and is why the markers exist.

docs.title: Reading it back
docs.text:
make build-status     # build records on $(BUILDER), with the node each ran on
make build-inspect    # duration, steps, cached steps, VCS revision
make layer-summary    # layer reuse per image, most recent build of each
make cache-summary    # compiler-cache size and the delta since last call

layer-summary is keyed by image, not by node. Which node a target ran on is an artefact of scheduling — the balancer moves targets between nodes run to run — so a per-node view answers "what did this machine last do" when the question is "how much of this image did we rebuild". The node is still shown, because it explains a low number: a target that moved nodes cannot use the previous node's local BuildKit cache and must refetch from Zot.

docs.title: When numbers are missing
docs.text: sccache counters are absent when a target was fully layer-cached. The build step never ran, so it printed no stats. That is correct, not a fault — and it is exactly the distinction the benchmark harness uses to separate a hot run that compiled from one that skipped the compile.

docs.title: Bake variables
docs.text:
rocm-bake.hcl declares 45 variables and is the single source for every value a build reads. The Makefile parses the variable blocks at make parse time and reads the defaults out, so make build-pytorch and a bare docker buildx bake pytorch always agree.

make list-vars prints the values actually in effect and is authoritative if this page has aged. .builders/check-defaults.py fails CI if a default is re-declared in the Makefile, or if the Makefile reads a variable that rocm-bake.hcl does not define.

Change a default by editing its variable block.

docs.title: Versions and refs
docs.text:
Variable Default PYTORCH_VERSION 2.15.0 ROCM_VERSION 10.1.0-full PYTHON_VERSION 3.14 TRITON_VERSION 3.9.0 TRITON_REF aad2a60d958f945420c5c40936b37d411fb02e89 AITER_REF v0.1.27 NIXL_REF v1.5.2 UCX_REF v1.22.0 VLLM_REF v0.32.0 CUPY_REF v14.2.0 LMCACHE_REF v0.5.6 RUST_VERSION 1.95 GIT_REF "" - a specific PyTorch ref to build

This table is generated from rocm-bake.hcl by make version-scrub, and make version-scrub-check fails CI if it drifts. make version-check compares each of these against the latest upstream release and against the wheels published in the registry.

The four serving-stack refs are release tags, never branches. A moving ref would be served from the layer cache indefinitely once built, so an "update" would silently be a no-op.

RUST_VERSION tracks the channel in vLLM's rust-toolchain.toml; v0.32 builds vllm/vllm-rs during setup.py.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text: Variable Default REGISTRY snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080 REGISTRY_NAME rocm-pytorch SOURCE_URL https://github.com/sbates130272/rocm-pytorch-build

docs.title: Architecture and build shape
docs.text:
Variable Default PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH gfx950 Semicolon-separated list; a list produces one fat binary USE_AITER ON USE_FLYDSL ON USE_FLASH_ATTENTION ON USE_ROCM_CK_SDPA_GFX12 "" RDNA4 Composable Kernel SDPA, new in PyTorch 2.15 and OFF upstream. ON takes effect only on a gfx12 RDNA4 target; anywhere else it stays OFF MAX_JOBS "" Empty derives it per node from MemAvailable PREBUILD_KERNELS "" Empty derives it from the architecture: 0 on RDNA, 2 on CDNA

See Multiple GFX targets for why the architecture decides the prebuild level, and why gfx125x is a special case.

docs.title: Compiler cache
docs.text:
Variable Default SCCACHE_WEBDAV_HOST snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net The nginx WebDAV store SCCACHE_WEBDAV_PORT 8081 SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT "" Composed from host and port; the Makefile supplies a resolved address SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX rocm-pytorch Namespace within the store SCCACHE_LOG warn debug reveals what "Cache errors" is counting SCCACHE_VERSION 0.19.0 0.8.0 is the floor for caching hipcc -x hip REQUIRE_SCCACHE 1 Refuse to compile when the store is unreachable FORCE_RECACHE false true recompiles everything, ignoring sccache

There is deliberately no SCCACHE_SERVER_PORT

Build containers reach their sccache server over a unix socket, because the builders run with network=host and a fixed port would be shared fleet-wide. See Caching. The host-level daemon in deploy-sccache.sh does use a port, which is fine — it is not in a container, and builds do not use it.

Note

Setting SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT yourself only affects a bare bake. The Makefile exports its own resolved-address form unconditionally.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Variable Default SDE_EPOCH 1700000000 SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH pinned into every image config SDE_BASE … SDE_CUPY "" Per-image overrides; empty means use SDE_EPOCH VCS_REF "" Supplied by the Makefile; gets a -dirty suffix BUILD_DATE "" Supplied by the Makefile as the commit's own timestamp

The nine per-image variables are SDE_BASE, SDE_PYTORCH, SDE_TRITON, SDE_AITER, SDE_RUNTIME, SDE_NIXL, SDE_VLLM, SDE_LMCACHE and SDE_CUPY. See Reproducibility for why the epoch is a constant rather than a date from git history.

docs.title: Caching and scheduling
docs.text: Variable Default CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX "" Empty writes the rolling tag; -ref refreshes the frozen baseline PUBLISHED_INPUTS "" 1 resolves sibling inputs from the registry instead of target: contexts RUN_ID dev Stamped into every BuildKit history record name

docs.title: Overriding without editing
docs.text:
# A different PyTorch version
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.PYTORCH_VERSION=2.13.0" pytorch

# A different ROCm base
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.ROCM_VERSION=7.14" pytorch

# A different registry
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.REGISTRY=myregistry.com:5000" \
  --set "*.args.REGISTRY_NAME=rocm-pytorch" pytorch

# A specific PyTorch ref
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.GIT_REF=refs/heads/develop" pytorch

# Build even though the compiler cache is unreachable
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.REQUIRE_SCCACHE=0" pytorch

--set on a bake variable is not the same as on an arg

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT, SCCACHE_LOG, PUBLISHED_INPUTS, RUN_ID, CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX and the SDE_* family are bake variables read from the environment. Using --set '*.args.X=…' for one of them adds the arg to every target and changes their cache keys. Use the environment:

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT=http://other-host:8081 \
  docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl pytorch

Through the Makefile, BAKE_EXTRA passes arbitrary flags to any target:

make build-pytorch BAKE_EXTRA='--set pytorch.args.SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=1700000001'

docs.text:
Thirteen targets. Every published repository is under snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/, elided below.

Each target emits three tags: a versioned one, :latest, and an immutable -g<sha> tag whenever VCS_REF is non-empty.

triton-wheel:3.9.0-10.1.0-full

nixl-wheel:v1.5.2-10.1.0-full-gfx950
vllm:v0.32.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950

make zot-tags REPO=rocm-pytorch/pytorch lists what is actually published.

docs.title: Two tags that are not what you would guess
docs.text:
triton-wheel carries no architecture and is version-prefixed. Triton is a compiler and publishes one noarch wheel, so the tag is 3.9.0-10.1.0-full, not 10.1.0-full-gfx950. wheelhouse.py parses it without a gfx component for the same reason.

pytorch-run publishes to runtime, with the architecture. It takes no PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH argument — it compiles nothing — but it COPYs the torch wheel out of pytorch, so what it ships is as architecture-specific as that wheel is. Without the architecture in the tag a gfx1201 runtime overwrote the gfx950 one and only the digest told them apart.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Group Members default pytorch-base, pytorch, pytorch-wheel, triton-wheel, aiter-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel wheels pytorch-wheel, triton-wheel, aiter-wheel, nixl-wheel, cupy-wheel, vllm-wheel, lmcache-wheel serving cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel

There is no all group. pytorch-test and pytorch-run are deliberately outside default — why.

wheels is separate because each of its members builds FROM an image that must already be published, so the group cannot run against a cold registry.

WHEEL_REPOS in the Makefile must match the wheels group; check-defaults.py fails CI if it drifts.

docs.title: Dockerfiles
docs.text:
Every Dockerfile lives in docker/, and the build context is always the repository root, so rocm-bake.hcl names them as docker/Dockerfile.<image>.

File Produces Dockerfile.base pytorch-base Dockerfile.pytorch pytorch, pytorch-wheel, pytorch-test Dockerfile.runtime pytorch-run Dockerfile.triton triton-wheel Dockerfile.aiter aiter-wheel Dockerfile.cupy cupy-wheel Dockerfile.nixl nixl-wheel Dockerfile.vllm vllm, vllm-wheel Dockerfile.lmcache lmcache, lmcache-wheel

A wheel target is the same Dockerfile built to its wheel stage, which is why pytorch-wheel inherits from pytorch, vllm-wheel from vllm, and lmcache-wheel from lmcache.

docs.text:

docs.title: Cache repositories
docs.text: Each target exports its layers to a *-cache repository, listed in Caching. Note that make clean-cache only removes base-cache, pytorch-cache, runtime-cache and cache locally — it does not cover the other six repositories, and the registry itself must be pruned separately.

docs.title: Make targets
docs.text:
make help is authoritative and prints the live list with the values currently in effect. This page is a map of the groups and the ones worth knowing about; a target missing here is not a target that does not exist.

Targets marked * in make help build and push to the registry, which needs the ci login.

make help          # every target, grouped
make list-vars     # every variable these targets read, with its value

docs.title: Registry (Zot)
docs.text:
Target zot-check Is the registry active and answering? zot-catalog List repositories zot-tags List tags for one repo — REPO=rocm-pytorch/base zot-wheels Published wheel artifacts, newest first — ZOT_TAGS=0 for all zot-wheelhouse The same with sizes, plus anything extracted into ./dist/wheels zot-logs Follow the registry's journal

Nothing here starts, stops or configures Zot. It is a bare-metal systemd service owned outside this repository.

docs.title: Compiler cache
docs.text: Target cache-summary Endpoint, size, disk, deltas and per-target hit rates cache-check Can every build node reach the store? cache-logs Follow the WebDAV access log layer-summary Layer reuse per image on its most recent build

docs.title: Builders
docs.text:
Target builder-setup All three builders builder-snoc-strix Local docker-container driver builder-snoc-think snoc-thinkstation, over SSH builder-snoc-gaming snoc-gaming, over SSH builder-snoc-pool All three as one buildx builder (little used — see below) builder-status Every builder and its nodes builder-health Which builders can take work builder-load CPU, cores and load per node of $(BUILDER) builder-logs buildkitd's own log: registry auth, GC, connection failures builder-restart Restart buildkitd on $(BUILDER), clearing a wedged build

builder-ensure gates every build target on builder-health, which is why a build fails fast against a dead node rather than hanging.

builder-restart drops that node's in-memory build state. The registry layer cache and the shared compiler cache are untouched, so the next build still picks up where it can.

docs.title: Watching a build
docs.text:
Target watch Live: history across all snoc-* builders, a tail of each running build, layer reuse and cache deltas build-status Build records on $(BUILDER), with the node each ran on build-logs What a build's steps printed — BUILD=<id>, default most recent build-inspect Duration, step count, cached steps, VCS revision build-stop Cancel builds started from this repository 
make watch
make watch WATCH_BUILDERS=snoc-think
make watch WATCH_LINES=40 WATCH_INTERVAL=2

Two logs, easy to confuse

build-logs is the output of the build's steps — what a RUN printed. builder-logs is the daemon underneath, and it is where a registry failure, a DNS failure or a cache problem shows up, often while the build itself just looks slow.

build-stop works off a PID file (/tmp/.rocm-build.pids) that every bake invocation and the balancer write to. Matching command lines with pgrep -f was unreliable: it killed the invoking shell, and it killed the sibling project's builds.

docs.title: Build and push
docs.text:
Build (no push) Push Target build-base push-base pytorch-base build-pytorch push-pytorch pytorch build-runtime push-runtime pytorch-run build-torch-wheel push-torch-wheel pytorch-wheel build-triton-wheel push-triton-wheel triton-wheel build-aiter-wheel push-aiter-wheel aiter-wheel build-cupy-wheel push-cupy-wheel cupy-wheel build-nixl-wheel push-nixl-wheel nixl-wheel build-vllm push-vllm vllm build-vllm-wheel push-vllm-wheel vllm-wheel build-lmcache push-lmcache lmcache build-lmcache-wheel push-lmcache-wheel lmcache-wheel build-serving push-serving the serving group build-all push-all the default group — push-wheels the wheels group

Every wheel has a build- form as well as a push- form. The build-only targets exist because the benchmark harness needs them: it dispatches through make build-<name>, and a push- target writes to the registry, which the credential helper cannot do unattended. Without them a cold measurement stopped at the first wheel that had no build-only target.

fetch-torch-wheel, fetch-triton-wheel, fetch-aiter-wheel, fetch-cupy-wheel, fetch-nixl-wheel, fetch-vllm-wheel and fetch-lmcache-wheel pull a published wheel artifact into ./dist.

cold-build builds COLD_TARGET (default pytorch) with neither layer cache nor compiler-cache hits.

build-all refuses BUILDER=snoc-pool

Scheduling makes every target its own bake invocation, so they cannot hand results to each other through target: contexts. Use push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool (scheduled, publishes) or build-all BUILDER=snoc-think (single builder, no push). See the balancer.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Target bench Run the harness — BENCH_SCENARIO=frozen\|cold\|warm\|hot\|all\|everything bench-report Render accumulated results as markdown bench-data Aggregate into dist/bench/bench.json for the docs site bench-publish Commit that onto gh-pages; PUSH=1 to push

See Performance.

docs.title: Performance runs
docs.text:
Target perf-plan Which builder each wheel would land on; builds nothing perf-run Cold parallel build of every wheel, fully instrumented perf-build The same instrumentation on a normal build — caches on, pushes perf-report Render the newest run as markdown plus SVG charts perf-serve Serve the newest run's interactive chart on :8090 perf-runs List collected runs, newest last

A different question from bench: the fleet flat out rather than one target in isolation. perf-run is a build from nothing; perf-build is the build you actually run, where the cost is almost entirely export rather than compute. See Instrumented fleet runs.

PERF_ARCH selects the architecture, PERF_TARGETS overrides what is built (default: bake's wheels group plus pytorch; ordering comes from the bake graph, so a subset still schedules correctly), and PERF_BIND narrows what perf-serve listens on — it binds every interface by default.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Target version-check Upstream releases vs published wheels vs our pins version-scrub Regenerate the version tables from rocm-bake.hcl version-scrub-check Fail if those generated tables are stale

version-check needs the network: gh for api.github.com and the tailnet for the registry. version-scrub reads rocm-bake.hcl and nothing else, which is what lets version-scrub-check gate every pull request in lint.yml.

The tables it generates live between <!-- BEGIN VERSIONS --> markers in README.md and in Bake variables. Bump a version in rocm-bake.hcl, run make version-scrub, commit both.

docs.text: Target validate Is the bake file parseable? bake-plan Print the resolved build plan as JSON list-vars Every variable these targets read, with its value and source clean Remove built images locally, for every architecture in ARCHES clean-cache Remove cache images locally — the registry must be pruned separately setup zot-check then builder-setup

docs.title: Variables worth knowing
docs.text:
Variable Default BUILDER snoc-strix Which builder, or snoc-pool for the balancer ARCHES gfx950 gfx1201 gfx1250 What arches-* fans out over PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH gfx950 The architecture for one build TELEMETRY 1 0 skips the metrics wrapper BAKE_EXTRA — Arbitrary extra flags passed to bake GPU_HOST snoc-thinkstation The machine with /dev/kfd REPO rocm-pytorch/base What zot-tags lists ZOT_TAGS 5 Tags per repo in zot-wheels; 0 for all BENCH_SCENARIO all Which benchmark scenario make bench runs

Some variables only work from the environment

make <target> VAR=value works for anything the Makefile reads. But SCCACHE_LOG, PUBLISHED_INPUTS, RUN_ID, CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX and the SDE_* overrides are read by bake, from the environment — so they need VAR=value make <target> instead.
